summary: Comments on the Remote Controlled Transmission and Echoing Telnet option described in RFC 560. It restates that the option lets the server control, on the user-to-server path, when characters are echoed and when they are sent, and then offers critique of the design.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 563 comments on the RCTE option described in RFC 560. The author argues that users should send characters using the rules they currently know, rather than pause until the server confirms new rules.

questions: what is the rcte telnet option
subtitle: A critique of how the RCTE TELNET option controls when typed characters are sent.

tldr.problem: RFC 560's RCTE option lets a server control which characters a user echoes and transmits, but the author says its transmission strategy can make the user wait for a server update.
tldr.mechanism: Davidson argues that the user should transmit according to the transmission-character set in effect when each character is typed, rather than wait for confirmation of a new set.
tldr.outcome: RFC 563 is a critique and alternative proposal, not a replacement specification.

today: The unit records RFC 563's status as Unknown and lists no updates or obsoleting RFCs. This document comments on the RCTE option described in RFC 560.

sections.title: Echoing and Sending Characters
sections.content:
RFC 560 describes Remote Controlled Transmission and Echoing (RCTE), under which a serving host controls when and which characters the user echoes and transmits on the user-to-server path. The RFC 563 author says the option's description is unclear about when characters should be sent.

He distinguishes character transmission from echoing. RFC 357's original remote-controlled echoing idea addressed the delay and confusion experienced by a person typing across a satellite link; the RFC says that original motivation did not consider processing efficiency or channel throughput.
sections.plainLanguage: Echoing controls when typed characters appear on the user's screen. Transmission controls when those characters travel to the remote host, and RFC 563 focuses on that second question.

sections.title: Why Waiting Can Add Delay
sections.content:
The author says a user may type several complete commands while waiting for the server's response to the first. Sending those commands as they are completed can overlap network transmission and server work. But if the server changes which characters trigger transmission, the user's view of the rule may differ from the server's for the time it takes the update to arrive.

Davidson objects that the RCTE example appears to make the user wait for the server to confirm the transmission-character set before sending subsequent characters. In his view, that adds a round-trip delay to the interaction and removes the benefit of typing ahead.
sections.plainLanguage: A user can type the next command while the server handles the last one. If the user must wait for updated sending rules, that overlap is lost and the exchange takes longer.

sections.title: The Proposed Transmission Rule
sections.content:
Davidson proposes deciding whether to transmit a character using the transmission-character set in effect when the user types it. The user would not wait for the server to confirm a later change before sending. The RFC's example shows that this can let typing and output proceed at the same time.

The author acknowledges that this strategy may send a packet that does not contain a complete command or may include more than one command. He argues that the alternative is worse for the user because it imposes an extra wait. The document also discusses unsolicited output and a problem involving full user buffers.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal is to apply the sending rule the user knows at the time of typing. That may send extra or incomplete data, but avoids waiting for confirmation of every rule change.

references.text: RFC 357, An Echoing Strategy for Satellite Links.
